text: In March, three Red Cross volunteers in eastern Congo were asked to bury the dead. A routine job, unrelated to Ebola.
Nobody knew there was an Ebola outbreak, because nobody had found it yet.
As of the seventeenth of August, that outbreak has five thousand one hundred and five confirmed cases, and two thousand four hundred and twenty confirmed deaths.
It is spreading substantially faster than any Ebola outbreak on record. So why now?
The answer most people have heard is that there is no vaccine. That is true. It is not the reason.
The outbreak was declared on the fifteenth of May, in Ituri province, north-eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo.
It has since reached fifty-four health zones across six provinces. More than ninety-seven percent of cases sit in three of them.
This is the first hundred days of five Ebola outbreaks, counted the same way. One of them is not like the others.
Congo passed a thousand confirmed cases forty days after the response began. The twenty eighteen outbreak, in the same country, took about two hundred and thirty-five days.
This is the largest Ebola outbreak in Congo's history. The previous largest, in twenty eighteen, had three thousand three hundred and seventeen confirmed cases.
But it is not the largest ever. West Africa, twenty fourteen to sixteen, had more than twenty-eight thousand. America's CDC calls this one the second largest on record.
Two thousand four hundred and twenty of those people have died. A case fatality rate of forty-seven percent, on the seventeenth of August.
At the end of July it was forty-four percent. Nobody is claiming the virus has changed. Testing and reporting move that number too.
Forty-seven percent is a frightening number. It describes people diagnosed with this disease, in the places where it is spreading. It does not describe your risk.
Ebola is not airborne, and it does not spread by casual contact. Experts do not consider Ebola viruses to have pandemic potential, for exactly that reason.
It spreads through direct contact with the blood or body fluids of someone sick, or someone who has died.
Which means the people most at risk are those caring for the sick, and those burying the dead.
Outside the region there has been one confirmed case, in France. None in the United States. The CDC puts the risk to the American public at low.
There is an Ebola vaccine. It has been used at scale, and it works.
It is called Ervebo, and it is licensed against Zaire ebolavirus.
This outbreak is not Zaire. It is a different species, called Bundibugyo.
The vaccine research foundation CEPI puts it plainly. There are no licensed vaccines for Bundibugyo virus.
Bundibugyo was identified in Uganda in two thousand and seven. Fifty-six cases. It appeared once more, in Congo, in twenty twelve. Both contained.
So no vaccine was ever licensed for it. That is the headline everyone has reported. It is real. It is also not what is driving this.
Containing Ebola has never actually depended on a vaccine. It depends on something less glamorous. Administration.
You find every person an infected patient has been in contact with.
You visit each of them, every day, for twenty-one days — the outer edge of the incubation period. You watch for a fever, and isolate before it spreads.
And every step assumes something. That you can locate them. That you can reach them safely. That when you knock, they open the door.
In eastern Congo, each of those assumptions fails independently.
These provinces host around four point four million internally displaced people. People who move cannot be revisited daily for three weeks.
The region has been in armed conflict for years, with multiple armed groups active across Ituri and North Kivu.
In late July, five response workers were briefly detained by an armed group. Health facilities have been attacked.
The CDC lists violence against health workers, and shortages of protective equipment. And one thing harder to fix. Lack of trust, and misinformation.
And the region was already hungry. The World Food Programme counts eight point seven million people at crisis levels of hunger in these provinces — before Ebola arrived.
The head of the World Health Organization described insecurity and population movement making it, in his words, nearly impossible to trace contacts.
Money has been committed. More than five hundred million dollars from the United States alone. Aid organisations say earlier American cuts weakened the response beforehand. Both are on the record.
But the shortage that matters is not only money. It is the ability to send someone to a door, safely, every day, for three weeks.
Which brings us back to March.
The three volunteers were Ajiko Chandiru Viviane, Sezabo Katanabo, and Alikana Udumusi Augustin, of the Congo Red Cross in Mongbwalu.
They handled the bodies on the twenty-seventh of March. All three were dead within seven weeks.
The first suspected case was recognised on the twenty-fourth of April, in a nurse.
Seven weeks separate that burial from the declaration on the fifteenth of May. Seven weeks in which the virus was moving, and no system existed to see it.
That is the gap. Not the vaccine. The seeing.
Uganda's share of this outbreak is already over.
It stayed in the capital. Twenty cases, no community spread. Declared over on the twenty-eighth of July.
So the answer to why now is this. Not because a vaccine is missing, though one is.
Because containment is an administrative act, attempted where administration is hardest.
There are trials. A treatment trial in Ituri. Two vaccine candidates entered first human trials this summer, in Britain and Canada.
None will arrive in time for this outbreak. What has to hold until they do is the knocking on doors.
